profile.title: Nutrition Assessment and Counseling for Shift-Work Eating in a 72-Year-Old Overnight Security Guard with Ischemic Heart Disease and Hypertension
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment with an anxious, low-health-literacy older adult whose shift-work schedule drives a pattern of skipped meals, heavy vending-machine/fast-food reliance, and inconsistent medication adherence despite reassuringly normal labs. The core teaching points are using motivational interviewing and teach-back to uncover hidden health literacy barriers without shame, recognizing a patient-vs-record mismatch between reported medication adherence and refill history, and building a realistic, culturally-grounded (church-community-leveraging) nutrition care plan for someone in the contemplation stage of change.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Holiday City-Berkeley, New Jersey, seated at his kitchen table before his overnight shift

patient.name: Arlie Farrell
patient.occupation: Overnight security guard at a retail distribution warehouse
patient.appearance: An older white man calling from his kitchen table, dressed in a worn flannel shirt, sitting with a mild forward-leaning posture. He looks tired with faint dark circles under his eyes, moves slowly and carefully as if his back is stiff, and jingles a set of keys in one hand when he gets nervous. A nasal, slightly hoarse voice is noticeable, and he occasionally sniffles or clears his throat.

persona.personality: Anxious, apologetic, and self-effacing; braces for criticism before it comes and tends to downplay his own struggles. Warm underneath the nervousness, especially when talking about his church family.
persona.communicationStyle: Soft-spoken, uses plain working-class language with no medical jargon. Apologizes frequently ('sorry, I know that's bad'), changes the subject when something feels too exposing, and jingles his keys when nervous. Responds well to warmth, patience, and simple explanations without numbers or percentages; shuts down or deflects if he feels lectured or rushed.
persona.emotionalState: Nervous and a little ashamed going into the visit, worried he's about to be scolded for his eating habits; brightens noticeably when talking about his church community or when treated gently rather than judged.
persona.background: Arlie grew up in a working-class family in rural New Jersey and left school after his GED to start working right away, which he's quietly proud of. He never married, has no kids, and has spent most of his adult life in physically demanding jobs, including decades driving a forklift before moving into warehouse security. He's worked overnight security at a retail distribution warehouse for years now, usually an 11pm-to-7am shift. He's single and lives in a household of four in Holiday City-Berkeley, New Jersey, though he doesn't consider the others close family. His real family, as he puts it, is his church congregation of over twenty years - he helps set up the Sunday potluck when his back allows, and a few older members check on him and bring him meals when he's having a bad flare. He keeps a small cooler in his truck for shift snacks, though it's rarely stocked with much beyond soda and old Halloween candy. He talks about his forklift days with a bit of pride when the conversation turns light.
speechExamples: Sorry, I know that's probably bad, huh?
I just eat whatever's around when I'm on shift, you know how it is.
Honestly I don't always get what those labels are trying to tell me, but don't tell anybody I said that.
My church folks, they're like my real family at this point.
I'm not trying to be difficult, I just... I don't want to mess something up.
concerns: Worried the student will scold him for his vending machine habits
Afraid his heart condition will get worse and he'll lose his job
Embarrassed that he doesn't always understand nutrition labels or his medication instructions

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment visit with Arlie Farrell, a 72-year-old man referred for help with his eating habits in the context of his heart condition, high blood pressure, and overnight work schedule. This is his first nutrition visit. Review his available health record information before the call, then conduct a diet history and counseling session, and complete an ADIME note afterward.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition counseling related to heart disease, blood pressure, and overnight shift-work eating
scenario.openingLine: Hi, yeah, sorry, I'm here. They told me I should talk to somebody about my eating, with the heart stuff and all. I work nights, so I know my eating's probably not the best.
tasks: Take a focused diet history covering his typical day, meal timing, and food choices, especially around his overnight shift schedule
Assess his health literacy and comfort with reading nutrition labels and food/medication instructions using a judgment-free, teach-back approach
Review available anthropometric, vital sign, and laboratory data as part of his nutrition assessment
Identify realistic, shift-work-friendly meal and snack strategies in partnership with the patient, using motivational interviewing to meet him where he is
Document an ADIME note that includes a nutrition diagnosis and patient-centered goals, noting any barriers or support systems relevant to his care

facts.says: My ankles puff up sometimes. I wondered if that little pill ain't working right.

facts.chart: Reports easy bruising, has not mentioned to his physician.
facts.says: I bruise kinda easy lately. Haven't said nothin' to the doctor about it though.

facts.chart: Denies nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Reports occasional stomach discomfort after taking ibuprofen on an empty stomach.
facts.says: My stomach's fine mostly, 'cept sometimes after I take one of them ibuprofen without eating nothing first.

facts.chart: No reported changes in bowel habits; reports increased urinary frequency related to diuretic use.
facts.says: Bathroom-wise I'm regular, 'cept that water pill makes me go a lot, which is a pain at work.

facts.chart: Reports disrupted sleep pattern due to overnight work, 5-6 hours daytime sleep.
facts.says: I sleep during the day, maybe five, six hours. It's never great sleep.

facts.says: I had bronchitis over the summer, then my sinuses acted up for a couple months, and I got a bladder infection back in December. All cleared up now.

facts.says: Had a cavity filled a while back, that's about it for my teeth.

facts.chart: History of streptococcal pharyngitis in June 2023, resolved with treatment.
facts.says: Had strep throat a couple years back. Got some medicine and it went away.

facts.chart: No prior surgeries reported.
facts.says: Never had surgery on anything, no.

facts.chart: No known drug or food allergies.
facts.says: No, I'm not allergic to nothin' that I know of.

facts.chart: Reports taking blood pressure medications 'pretty regular.'
facts.says: I take my blood pressure pills pretty regular, I try real hard not to miss 'em.

facts.chart: Reports sometimes skipping hydrochlorothiazide before work shifts due to bathroom access concerns.
facts.says: Sometimes I skip that water pill before I go in, 'cause I don't want to be running to the bathroom all night at work.

facts.says: I got a multivitamin my sister got me, I take it when I remember. And I keep some antacids and a nose spray around too.

facts.says: My weight's been about the same, I ain't really lost or gained much that I noticed.

facts.chart: Works full-time overnight security shifts, approximately 11pm-7am, at a retail warehouse
facts.says: I do security overnight at the warehouse, so I'm up all night and crashed out most of the day.

facts.chart: Lives in a household of four; reports limited close contact with family members
facts.says: I live with some folks, there's four of us in the house, but it's not like we're close or anything. I mostly keep to myself.

facts.chart: Never married, no children
facts.says: Never got married, never had kids. Just been me, working, mostly.

facts.says: My church, they're like my family. Been going there over twenty years. Sunday potlucks are the best meal I get all week, honestly.

facts.chart: Reports pastor and congregation members check on him and sometimes bring meals when his back pain is severe
facts.says: Pastor calls to check on me sometimes. And a couple of the older ladies, if my back's real bad, they'll drop off a plate.

facts.says: I just want to keep working as long as my back lets me. I don't want to be a burden on nobody.

facts.says: Guy I worked with, he had a heart attack right there on shift. I think about that. I'm scared it could be me next.

facts.says: I help set up the Sunday meal at church. I'd hate to not be able to do that no more.

facts.says: Those directions on the bottles, they're just confusing, you know? I don't always get what they mean.

facts.says: [If pressed gently] ...honestly, I never was much good at reading all them little numbers. I just kind of guess, or I say I understand so nobody thinks less of me.

facts.says: [Reluctantly] There was one time... I went to the ER, chest felt real tight. I never told my regular doctor. Didn't want them thinking I couldn't handle my job.

facts.says: Standing at the stove too long, my back just can't take it most days.

facts.chart: Reports limited household income makes fresh produce feel unaffordable
facts.says: Fresh vegetables and all that, it adds up fast. On my budget it feels like a luxury sometimes.

facts.says: Never smoked a day in my life, and I don't really drink either.

facts.chart: Reports sedentary lifestyle outside of work; walks warehouse floor during shifts but limited exercise on days off due to back pain
facts.says: I walk around the warehouse all night, that's about it. On my days off, my back's usually too sore to do much.

facts.chart: Mentions pride in having been trained to operate a forklift earlier in his career
facts.says: Learned to drive a forklift years back. Still proud of that, if I'm honest.

actions.name: Conduct 24-hour dietary recall
actions.result: Patient describes: skips breakfast (asleep), small lunch (sandwich or leftovers), large dinner before shift (meat, starch, sometimes canned corn or green beans), then vending machine chips/pretzels/candy bars and 2-3 sodas through the night shift, fast food burger-and-fries on the drive home around 6am; coffee with cream and sugar throughout the day, rarely plain water

actions.name: Assess usual meal timing and pattern around work schedule
actions.result: Patient reports sleeping through most mornings, eating a small lunch after waking, a large dinner before his 11pm shift, grazing overnight, and stopping for fast food on the drive home around 6am; says his break schedule at work is unpredictable and limits planning

actions.name: Assess fluid and beverage intake
actions.result: Patient reports several cups of coffee daily with cream and sugar, 2-3 cans of soda per shift, rarely drinks plain water unless reminded

actions.name: Assess physical activity level
actions.result: Patient reports walking the warehouse floor during shifts but otherwise sedentary; says back pain limits exercise on days off

actions.name: Screen alcohol use (AUDIT-C)
actions.result: AUDIT-C score 0; patient reports essentially no alcohol use, never smoked tobacco

actions.name: Assess food access, budget, and kitchen/cooking barriers
actions.result: Patient reports limited income makes fresh produce feel like a luxury, chronic back pain makes standing at the stove difficult, and he relies on a truck cooler usually stocked with soda and old candy rather than real food

actions.name: Assess health literacy using plain-language teach-back
actions.result: When asked to read a sample nutrition facts label aloud and explain it back, patient becomes quiet, says 'I think I get it,' struggles to identify sodium or sugar content, and visibly relaxes when the label is reviewed together verbally instead of being handed to him to read alone

actions.name: Screen readiness to change using stages-of-change framework
actions.result: Patient endorses knowing his eating habits 'aren't great' and expresses some desire to change but is unsure where to start and voices fear of failing or being judged, consistent with the contemplation stage

actions.name: Assess social support and community resources relevant to eating
actions.result: Patient describes his church congregation of over 20 years as his closest support, mentions Sunday potlucks with home-cooked casseroles and baked ham, and says a few older members bring him meals when his back is bad; reports limited contact with biological family

actions.name: Review problem list and visit history for recent acute illness
actions.result: See acute care/urgent visit history note

actions.name: Review understanding of current medication purposes and schedule
actions.result: Patient can name a few pills by appearance ('the water pill,' 'the heart ones') but is unsure what several are for, says the two prescription pain pills 'look about the same to him' on the label, and mentions he sometimes guesses the timing when instructions aren't clear

objectives.text: Elicit a focused diet history that captures shift-work-driven meal timing, skipped meals, and reliance on vending machine/fast food, including fluid and caffeine intake.
Assess health literacy in a judgment-free, teach-back manner to uncover difficulty reading nutrition labels and medication instructions without triggering shame.
Integrate anthropometric, vital sign, and laboratory data into the nutrition assessment, recognizing that normal/controlled labs do not negate dietary risk.
Use motivational interviewing to engage a patient in the contemplation stage, validating effort and addressing fear of judgment to build readiness for change.
Identify barriers to healthy eating (chronic pain limiting cooking, limited income, irregular schedule) and existing supports (church community) to inform realistic, patient-centered goals.
Recognize discrepancies between patient-reported medication adherence and objective pharmacy records, and consider their relevance to nutrition counseling and interdisciplinary communication.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Undesirable food choices and irregular meal pattern related to overnight shift-work schedule, chronic pain limiting food preparation, and limited health literacy, as evidenced by heavy reliance on vending-machine/fast-food intake, skipped breakfast, high added sugar and sodium intake, and inconsistent antihypertensive adherence.
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Undesirable food choices (NB-1.7) related to shift-work schedule and limited understanding of label reading
Nutrition diagnosis: Inconsistent carbohydrate/sodium intake related to irregular meal timing and reliance on convenience foods
Nutrition-related: Medication/food interaction risk (e.g., antacid or grapefruit-type concerns) - not primary focus here
Behavioral: Low health literacy affecting ability to self-manage diet and medications (contributing factor, not itself a nutrition diagnosis)
Psychosocial: Contemplation-stage readiness to change with fear of judgment, a barrier to be addressed via MI rather than a diagnosis
keyFindings: Lipid panel and CBC within normal limits despite poor dietary pattern (reassuring but does not reflect intake quality)
Diet history reveals skipped breakfast, small lunch, large pre-shift dinner, overnight grazing on chips/pretzels/candy/soda, fast food on drive home
Minimal vegetable intake (only canned corn, green beans tolerated), minimal plain water intake, heavy sweetened coffee intake
Patient reports taking blood pressure medications 'pretty regular' but refill/adherence record shows gaps in hydrochlorothiazide fills consistent with frequent skipped doses
Patient reluctantly discloses difficulty reading nutrition labels and medication instructions, previously undisclosed to any provider
Patient reluctantly discloses an ER visit in the past year for chest tightness never reported to his regular doctor
Strong church-based social support network with potential to reinforce healthier choices (potlucks, check-ins)
plan: Complete ADIME note: Assessment (24-hr/typical day diet history, anthropometrics, labs, medication list, psychosocial/readiness-to-change), Diagnosis (PES statement centered on undesirable food choices related to shift-work schedule and limited health literacy as evidenced by diet history findings), Intervention (plain-language, teach-back based education; practical shift-friendly snack/meal swaps; label-reading support without shame; leverage church potlucks for healthy dish ideas), Monitoring/Evaluation (follow-up diet recall, weight, BP trend, patient-reported confidence/readiness)
Use teach-back to confirm understanding of any education given rather than handouts with numbers/percentages

Offer concrete, low-literacy-friendly strategies for the overnight shift: pre-packed cooler swaps (nuts, cheese sticks, fruit, water) instead of soda/candy; a modest pre-shift meal instead of one large heavy dinner; limiting cream/sugar in coffee gradually
Validate his effort and fear of failure using motivational interviewing; avoid judgmental language about vending machine or fast food habits
Explore and gently normalize his difficulty with labels; offer to walk through a label together rather than hand him material to read alone

Identify a referral or communication back to his primary care team regarding the medication adherence gap and the unreported chest tightness/ER visit, since this is outside dietetics scope to manage directly but important to flag
Discuss the church potluck community as a support system - encourage him to bring a modified-healthier dish and ask about accountability check-ins
Set one or two small, patient-chosen, realistic goals (e.g., swapping one nightly soda for water, adding a vegetable at dinner) rather than a full overhaul
redFlags: Unreported chest tightness and an unreported ER visit for cardiac symptoms - needs communication to his PCP/cardiology team, not managed by dietitian but must be flagged for follow-up
Inconsistent antihypertensive adherence (HCTZ gaps, amlodipine missed doses) with reported ankle swelling - relevant to overall cardiovascular risk, should be communicated to prescribing provider
Confusion between two opioid-containing pain medications raising risk of inadvertent overdose - outside nutrition scope but warrants referral/flag to care team
Low health literacy affecting safe self-management of both diet and medications - needs plain-language approach and possible referral to health literacy or care coordination resources
educationPoints: Why consistent meal timing (even on an overnight schedule) helps with energy, blood pressure control, and avoiding the heavy end-of-night vending habit
Simple, affordable snack swaps that travel well in a truck cooler for overnight shifts (e.g., unsalted nuts, string cheese, fruit, plain crackers, water)
How to identify high-sodium or high-sugar packaged snacks without needing to read a full nutrition label (e.g., comparing short ingredient lists, choosing recognizable whole foods)
The role of vegetables he already tolerates (canned corn, green beans) in building toward a more balanced plate, without forcing disliked vegetables
Gentle reassurance that his lab values look good now, and that building sustainable habits now helps keep them that way, rather than focusing on past 'bad' choices
Framing small, patient-chosen changes (one soda swapped for water, one vegetable added) as meaningful progress rather than an all-or-nothing overhaul

mismatches.patientClaim: Reports taking blood pressure medications 'pretty regular' (h21)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows hydrochlorothiazide refill gaps consistent with frequent missed doses over the past 6 months
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often overestimates actual medication-taking behavior; reviewing objective refill records can reveal gaps that affect nutrition-medication counseling (e.g., sodium/fluid guidance, timing around diuretic use) and should prompt non-judgmental exploration rather than assumption of full adherence.
